extracted.intended_audience: federal regulatory analysts and agency rulewriters (heads of executive agencies and establishments)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing regulatory analyses to support major Federal rulemakings, including how to identify need for regulation, select and evaluate alternatives, and measure and report benefits and costs (BCA and CEA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Key elements of a regulatory analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A good regulatory analysis should include the following three basic elements: (1) a statement of the need for the proposed action, (2) an examination of alternative approaches, and (3) an evaluation of the benefits and costs—quantitative and qualitative—of the proposed action and the main alternatives identified by the analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how actions are linked to expected benefits; identify a baseline (normally 'no action'); identify undesirable side-effects and ancillary benefits; include discussion of non-quantified as well as quantified benefits and costs; present summary of benefit and cost estimates for each alternative; provide an executive summary and a standardized accounting statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrating the need for Federal regulatory action
rubrics_metrics.description: Before recommending Federal regulatory action, an agency must demonstrate that the proposed action is necessary and 'identify the problem that it intends to address' and assess the significance of that problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe statutory authority and the extent of discretion; explain whether action addresses market failure or other compelling public need; present qualitative and where feasible quantitative description of the problem; show that government intervention is likely to do more good than harm; evaluate intangible rationales by presenting strengths and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and justify the baseline
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify a baseline against which benefits and costs are defined; this normally will be a 'no action' baseline, although comparisons to a 'next best' alternative can be useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State clearly what world you compare the rule to; for the least stringent alternative, incremental effects equal the totals; use baselines consistently across alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of market failures and other social purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the issue results from market failures (externalities, market power, inadequate/asymmetric information) or other social purposes (improving government functioning, redistribution, anti-discrimination, privacy, personal freedom).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe market failures qualitatively and quantitatively where feasible; document information-processing problems carefully; consider alternative non-regulatory means if market failure is uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption against certain economic regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: A particularly demanding burden of proof is required to justify regulations such as price controls in competitive markets, production or sales quotas in competitive markets, mandatory uniform quality standards if voluntary measures suffice, and controls on entry into employment or production (with narrow exceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid such regulations unless strong justification exists; explain why alternatives (voluntary standards, disclosure) are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explore a range of alternative regulatory approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Once Federal action is appropriate, consider multiple alternatives (statutory choices, different compliance dates, different enforcement methods, degrees of stringency, differential requirements by firm size or region, performance vs design standards, market-oriented and informational approaches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminarily eliminate obviously unsuitable options then analyze a manageable set; balance thoroughness with analytic capacity; evaluate modifications of regulatory attributes and examine likely interaction effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance standards preferred to design standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Performance standards express requirements in terms of outcomes rather than specifying means; they generally give regulated parties flexibility and can be superior to engineering or design standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for cost savings from flexibility and any monitoring or compliance costs required to ensure performance standards are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider market-oriented approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Market-oriented approaches using economic incentives—fees, penalties, subsidies, marketable permits or offsets, changes in liability or property rights, bonds/insurance/warranties—should be explored as alternatives to direct controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate potential cost reductions and distributional effects (e.g., ABT programs for emissions), and guard against unacceptable local outcomes like pollution 'hot spots'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider informational measures as less intrusive alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: If the problem arises from inadequate/asymmetric information, informational remedies (standardized testing/rating systems, mandatory disclosure, government provision of information) often should be preferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate costs of gathering/communicating information, displacement of other information, misinterpretation or ignoring of information; consider least intrusive informational alternative sufficient to meet objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Benefit-Cost Analysis (BCA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where all benefits and costs can be quantified and expressed in monetary units, BCA should be used to provide a common measure to evaluate alternatives and identify the alternative that maximizes net benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure incremental benefits and costs of successively more stringent alternatives; do not use benefit-cost ratios alone to determine net benefits; when some benefits cannot be monetized, measure in physical units or describe qualitatively and consider threshold analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Cost-Effectiveness Analysis (CEA)
rubrics_metrics.description: CEA should be prepared for major rulemakings where primary benefits are public health and safety and a valid effectiveness measure exists; perform CEA when some primary benefits cannot be monetized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer final outcome measures (lives saved, life-years saved) to intermediate outputs; construct cost and effectiveness measures carefully; present incremental cost-effectiveness relative to baseline and more stringent alternatives; beware of averages and dominated alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to use both BCA and CEA
rubrics_metrics.description: A major rulemaking should be supported by both BCA and CEA wherever possible—CEA for primary health/safety outcomes when effectiveness measure exists and BCA when valid monetary values can be assigned to primary outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For other major rulemakings, carry out a BCA; if some primary benefit categories cannot be monetized, also conduct a CEA; if no quantified information exists, present a qualitative discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measuring costs in CEA (net costs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include all relevant costs to society (public and private). The numerator in a cost-effectiveness ratio should reflect net costs, defined as gross compliance costs minus any cost savings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid double-counting effects in numerator and denominator (e.g., don't subtract monetary life-extension value if life-years are used as denominator); subtract monetized ancillary benefits when primary effectiveness measure cannot be monetized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing and justifying effectiveness measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Select effectiveness measures that capture final outcomes (lives saved, life-years, QALYs, equivalent lives) and explain the choice; when outcomes vary in quality (e.g., wetland quality), the measure should reflect variability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When several beneficial outcomes exist, weighting is required to integrate; consider integrated measures (QALYs) but be explicit about their assumptions and limitations; make adjustments to ensure fair treatment of population segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incremental analysis and dominance principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine incremental benefits/costs for alternatives and use incremental cost-effectiveness to avoid errors from average comparisons; eliminate inferior alternatives using strong and weak dominance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether alternatives are mutually exclusive or combinable; consider regulatory budget constraints when combining alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of non-quantified benefits and costs
rubrics_metrics.description: When important benefits and costs cannot be expressed in monetary units, identify and discuss them; perform threshold or 'break-even' analysis to evaluate significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicate which non-quantified effects are most important and why; if threshold analysis shows results are sensitive, explain and consider further analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: A good analysis is transparent so a qualified third party can see how estimates and conclusions were derived; state assumptions such as time horizon and discount rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide sensitivity analyses, specific references to data sources, appendices documenting models, and results of formal uncertainty analyses; include an executive summary and standardized accounting statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of risk and uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide expected-value estimates and distributions where available; when only bounds are provided, use 95 and 5 percent confidence bounds if possible; report alternative assumptions if estimates are sensitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principles of full disclosure apply; where uncertainty critically affects inferences, describe benefits and costs under plausible alternative assumptions and provide documentation or footnotes as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discounting and time presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Present undiscounted streams of benefits and costs for each year of the analytic time horizon and annualized benefits and costs using real discount rates of 3 and 7 percent; report all monetized effects in 2001 dollars and convert using the GDP deflator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin the annualized stream in the year the final rule begins to have effects; show undiscounted and discounted figures for transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision and rounding of estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported estimates should reflect the precision in the analysis; e.g., $220 million implies rounding to the nearest $10 million (precision +/- $5 million), $222 million implies rounding to nearest $1 million (+/- $0.5 million).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose rounding consistent with implied precision and document rounding rules used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate reporting of transfers
rubrics_metrics.description: Report transfers separately and avoid misclassifying transfer payments as benefits or costs; transfers are redistributions without direct change in aggregate social welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish transfers from federal budget actions and from transfers between non-governmental parties; use categories sufficient to describe major redistributive effects; identify transfers that have significant efficiency effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify distributional effects and sectoral impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify portions of benefits, costs, and transfers received by State, local, and tribal governments; to the extent feasible, identify effects on small businesses, wages, and economic growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that rules with annual costs below $1 billion are likely to have minimal effect on economic growth; where possible quantify or describe distributional consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized statutory and executive-order analytical requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether specialized analyses are required by law or Executive Order (e.g., Regulatory Flexibility Act for small entities; Unfunded Mandates Act for >$100M; Paperwork Reduction Act for information collections; NEPA; Executive Order 13045 on children; Executive Order 13211 on energy impacts; Information Quality Guidelines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare required RFAs, statements of unfunded mandates, information collection justifications and obtain OMB approval as needed; consult agency offices (CIO, Chief Counsel for Advocacy, etc.) and relevant guidance memos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting statement and reporting format
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide an accounting statement with tables reporting benefit and cost estimates for each major final rule; report estimates within three categories: monetized quantified, quantified but not monetized, and qualitative (not quantified or monetized).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid double-counting; present undiscounted streams and annualized estimates; include footnotes for documentation, warnings, or alternative assumptions; provide alternative primary estimates where mortality valuation differs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultation and stakeholder engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek opinions of those who will be affected and those with specialized knowledge; consultation should not be limited to the final stages and early consultation can be especially helpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use consultation to ensure analyses address relevant issues and to access pertinent data; consider SBREFA procedures when rules may significantly affect small businesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of timing and compliance dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate different compliance dates because timing can substantially affect benefits and costs; delayed implementation may reduce benefits or reduce costs if lead time is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze alternatives with different lead times and implementation schedules to identify cost-effective timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of enforcement and monitoring options
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify alternative enforcement frameworks (Federal, State, local; on-site inspections; periodic reporting; penalties) and select methods that provide appropriate incentives at reasonable cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider random or parametric monitoring when less expensive and nearly as effective as continuous monitoring; include enforcement costs in overall cost estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different requirements by firm size and geography
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider setting differentiated requirements for large vs small firms and for different geographic regions when benefits or costs vary significantly by size or region.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base differentiation on estimated cost differences or expected benefits; remember Regulatory Flexibility Act triggers for significant impacts on substantial numbers of small entities; evaluate regional tradeoffs including potential for fragmented regulation vs harmonization.
